REV A · SENSE · DECIDE · ACT

Six EE Projects That
Think For Themselves
Rovers, arms, legs, eyes, and hands — six complete robots that run the loop every real robot
runs: sense, decide, act. From a rover that avoids walls on its own, to an arm that solves its
own joint angles, to a quadruped that walks, to a rover that maps a room it has never seen.
Commodity parts; real robotics engineering.

build robots — a Build List field guide
1 / 15
WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand the sense-plan-act loop, distance sensing (ultrasonic time-of-flight, IR reflectance), differential-
drive steering, and behavior-based control. That is the foundation of mobile robotics and embedded control.
→the job this maps to: mobile robotics & embedded systems — robot-vacuum, warehouse-AMR, and consumer-robotics
teams.
// how it works
Sense-plan-act: The robot reads its sensors, applies a rule to decide a motion, drives the motors, and repeats many
times a second. The entire behavior emerges from that tight loop — no global map required.
Ultrasonic ranging: An HC-SR04 emits a 40 kHz ping and times the echo; distance is the speed of sound times the time,
halved. It gives you a “how far to the thing ahead” number tens of times a second.
IR reflectance: Cheap IR sensors detect a nearby obstacle (or a line or edge) by bounced infrared. Mounted at the
corners, they catch what the forward ultrasonic misses.
Differential drive: Two independently driven wheels (plus a caster) steer by speed difference: equal speeds go straight,
unequal speeds turn, opposite spin turns in place. It is the simplest steerable platform there is.
Behavior rules: A priority list of simple behaviors — if something is close ahead, back up and turn; else if a side sensor

fires, veer away; else drive forward — produces surprisingly lifelike wandering. This is behavior-based (subsumption)
control.

■ P R O J E C T 0 1
Reactive Rover
A rover that senses walls and steers itself — the sense-plan-act loop in its simplest form

$35
beginner
1 weekend
// why this matters
Every robot, from a vacuum to a Mars rover, runs the same loop: sense the world, decide what to do, act, repeat. A reactive
rover is the purest version — an ultrasonic and a pair of IR sensors feed a few simple rules that steer two motors, and the

machine roams a room avoiding walls and furniture with no map and no plan. It is the cheapest way to build something that
behaves on its own, the payoff is immediate (it just drives off), and it is the chassis and control skeleton every later project
in this guide builds on.

Build and drive the chassis
Assemble the 2WD chassis, wire the motor driver, and drive forward, back, and turn from code. Confirm the wheels
spin the right way.
Read the ultrasonic
Mount the HC-SR04 facing forward, trigger a ping, time the echo, and print distance. Wave a hand in front and watch
the number track.
Add the IR sensors
Mount IR sensors at the front corners and read them. Confirm they trigger on a nearby wall or hand.
Write the behavior rules

Implement the priority rules: close ahead means back up and turn, a side sensor means veer, otherwise forward. Let
it loose in a room and watch it avoid furniture.
Tune and make it lifelike
Adjust thresholds, turn durations, and speeds until it roams smoothly without getting stuck. Add a random turn
direction so it explores — your first autonomous robot.

build robots — a Build List field guide
3 / 15
WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand forward and inverse kinematics, joint-space versus Cartesian-space control, servo coordination,
workspace limits, and trajectory smoothing. Kinematics and manipulation are core to industrial and collaborative
robotics.
→the job this maps to: robotics and manipulation engineering — industrial-robot, cobot, and automation teams.
// how it works
Forward kinematics: Given the joint angles and link lengths, trigonometry tells you where the gripper ends up. It is the
easy direction, and it is how you verify your model against the real arm.
Inverse kinematics: Given a target (x, y, z), you solve backward for the joint angles. For a 4-axis arm: base rotation from
the target’s bearing, then a planar two-link triangle (shoulder and elbow) solved with the law of cosines, then the wrist
to level the gripper.
The two-link triangle: The shoulder, elbow, and target form a triangle whose sides are your link lengths and the distance
to the target. The law of cosines gives the elbow angle; a little more trig gives the shoulder. That is the heart of the
solution.
Joint limits and workspace: Servos only rotate so far and links have fixed lengths, so only a region of space is
reachable. Your IK must check reachability and respect limits, or you command the impossible.
Smooth motion: Jumping servos straight to a new angle is jerky. Interpolating between poses over time (in joint space,
or along a straight Cartesian path) makes motion smooth and predictable — the beginning of trajectory planning.

■ P R O J E C T 0 2
Robot Arm with Inverse Kinematics
Tell the arm an X, Y, Z and it works out every joint angle itself — pick and place, from math

$60
intermediate
1–2 weekends
// why this matters
A robot arm looks simple until you try to move its hand to a specific point in space: you have to solve, in reverse, what every
joint angle must be to put the gripper there. That is inverse kinematics, and it is the difference between a servo puppet and

a robot you command in coordinates. Build a 4-axis arm, derive its geometry, implement IK, and you can type a position and
watch it reach there, then pick up an object and place it somewhere else. It is the classic centrepiece of robotics, the
flagship of this guide, and a direct lesson in the math every industrial arm runs.

// build steps
Why solve inverse kinematics instead of driving joints by hand? Joint angles are not how tasks are described — a task
says “put the gripper here.” IK translates a Cartesian target into joint angles automatically, so you can command
positions, follow paths, and place objects precisely. Without it, an arm is a puppet; with it, it is programmable.
Why a closed-form geometric solution instead of a numeric solver? A 4-axis arm with a planar geometry has a clean
trigonometric solution: rotate the base to the target’s bearing, then solve the two-link triangle with the law of cosines. It

is exact, instant, and easy to reason about — and it teaches the geometry. Numeric solvers matter for six or more axes
and redundancy.
Why must IK check reachability? The arm can only reach points within its link lengths and joint limits; some targets are
too far, too close, or need an impossible elbow angle. IK must validate the solution and clamp or reject bad targets, or
the arm slams into itself — the practical discipline real controllers enforce.
Assemble and centre the arm

Build the arm, mount servos at their mid-positions, and drive each joint individually. Confirm range and direction for
base, shoulder, elbow, and wrist.
Measure and model
Measure your link lengths and joint offsets, and write forward kinematics. Command known angles and check the
gripper lands where the math predicts.
Implement inverse kinematics
Solve the base bearing, the two-link triangle with the law of cosines, and the wrist. Command an (x, y, z) and watch
the arm reach it. Fix the sign errors — there will be some.
Add limits and smoothing
Reject unreachable targets, clamp joint limits, and interpolate between poses so moves are smooth. Trace a straight
line and a circle in the air.
Pick and place
Add the gripper, command a sequence — move above an object, descend, grip, lift, move, release — and place
objects from one spot to another. Film it from the side.

build robots — a Build List field guide
6 / 15
WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand leg inverse kinematics, gait generation and phasing, static stability (support polygons), servo torque
budgeting, and coordinating many actuators in real time. Legged locomotion is one of the most demanding — and
most exciting — corners of robotics.
→the job this maps to: legged robotics and mechatronics — robot-dog, humanoid, and research-lab robotics teams.
// how it works
BUILD NOTE
Print a proven open-source quadruped frame rather than designing your own, use decent metal-gear servos (cheap
plastic ones strip under load), and power the servos from a dedicated high-current supply. Get one leg’s IK working
standing still before you attempt a single step.
Legs are arms: Each leg has three joints — hip abduction, hip pitch, knee — and placing a foot at an (x, y, z) is the same
inverse-kinematics problem as the arm, solved twelve times over for four legs.
Gaits: A gait is the pattern of which legs are in the air and which are on the ground. A creep moves one leg at a time
(slow, always stable); a trot moves diagonal pairs together (faster, needs balance). Phasing the legs correctly is what
makes walking work.
Stability: When a leg lifts, the body must stay balanced over the remaining feet. The support polygon — the area under
the grounded feet — must contain the centre of mass, or the robot tips. Shifting the body before lifting a leg is the trick.
Swing and stance: A stepping leg swings forward through the air; the grounded legs stroke backward together to push
the body forward. Coordinating swing and stance across all legs, cycle after cycle, is the gait engine.

Torque and timing: Twelve servos moving under load draw serious current and must move smoothly and in sync. A
dedicated supply, sensible speeds, and a fixed-rate control loop are the difference between a walk and a twitching heap.
▸

■ P R O J E C T 0 3
Quadruped Walker
Four legs, twelve servos, and a gait that actually walks — the robot everyone stops to watch

$90
advanced
2 weekends
// why this matters
Nothing stops a scroll like a small four-legged robot walking across a table. Each leg is a little robot arm with its own inverse
kinematics, and walking is the art of moving them in a coordinated rhythm — a gait — while keeping the body balanced over

the feet still on the ground. Build a 12-servo quadruped, solve leg IK, and implement a creep or trot gait, and you have a
machine that walks, turns, and stands up on its own. It is the most ambitious build in this guide, a genuine mechatronics
and control challenge, and the same fundamentals behind every legged robot from research labs to robot dogs.

// interview questions
Build and calibrate one leg
Assemble a single leg, mount its three servos, and calibrate their zero positions. Drive each joint and confirm range.
Solve leg IK
Implement inverse kinematics for one leg and command foot positions. Move the foot through a square in the air and
confirm it tracks. Then replicate to all four legs.
Stand up
Command all four feet to a standing stance and lift the body off the ground. Balance the stance and tune the servo
speeds so it rises smoothly.
Implement a creep gait

Move one leg at a time — shift the body over the other three, swing one leg forward, set it down, repeat. Get it to take
slow, stable steps forward.
Trot and turn
Move to a diagonal-pair trot for speed, add turning by asymmetric strokes, and add a remote for direction. Now walk
it across the table and film it.

build robots — a Build List field guide
8 / 15
WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand image capture and processing, object detection (colour segmentation, face and feature detection),
turning detection into a control error, visual servoing, and the latency and robustness issues of real-world vision.
Perception plus control is the core of modern robotics.

→the job this maps to: robot perception and computer-vision engineering — autonomous-vehicle, delivery-robot, and
industrial-vision teams.
// how it works
Capture and detect: A camera grabs frames; OpenCV finds the target — simplest via colour segmentation (threshold in
HSV for a coloured ball), or a face or feature detector. The output is a bounding box or centroid in pixel coordinates.
From pixels to error: The target’s horizontal offset from image centre is your steering error; its apparent size is your
range error. Perception has become two numbers a controller can use.
Visual servoing: Feed those errors into control loops: turn toward the target to zero the horizontal error, drive forward or
back to hold the size at a setpoint. The robot now tracks and follows — a control loop closed through a camera.
Latency and robustness: Vision is slow and noisy compared to a sensor: frames take time, detection jitters, lighting
changes ruin colour thresholds. Filtering the detection and tuning gains for the latency are what make tracking smooth.

Stepping up: Swap colour segmentation for a lightweight neural detector (a MobileNet-class model on a Pi) and the
same pipeline tracks people or objects by class — the path to real-world perception.
▸

■ P R O J E C T 0 4
Vision-Guided Tracking Robot
A robot that sees a target and follows it across the room — perception meets control

$45
intermediate
1–2 weekends
// why this matters
A robot that can see is a robot that can do almost anything, and the simplest vision task — find a thing and follow it —
teaches the whole perception-to-action pipeline. Put a camera on your rover or a pan-tilt head, detect a coloured object (or

a face) with OpenCV, and steer the robot to keep it centred and at a set distance. The result follows you around a room, and
the pipeline (capture, detect, compute error, control) is exactly what robot vacuums, delivery robots, and industrial vision
systems run. It is the bridge from blind reactive behavior to robots that understand what is in front of them.

// interview questions
Stream and view video
Set up the camera and confirm you can capture frames and display them (or stream to a laptop). Check the frame
rate — it sets your control rate.
Detect a coloured target
Threshold in HSV to segment a brightly coloured ball, find its contour, and draw its centroid and bounding box. Tune
the thresholds for your lighting.
Compute errors
Calculate horizontal offset from centre and target size each frame. Print both and move the ball around to see them
respond.
Close the loop
Drive the base (or pan-tilt) to zero the offset and hold the size at a setpoint. Tune gains until it tracks smoothly
without oscillating.
Follow you
Let it follow the ball (or you) around the room. Test changing light and speed, add filtering, then try a face or neural
detector for a bigger challenge.

build robots — a Build List field guide
10 / 15
WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand tactile and force sensing (FSRs, load cells), compliant gripper design, closed-loop force control
versus position control, grasp detection, and the mechanics of gentle manipulation — core to manipulation and soft-
robotics engineering.

→the job this maps to: manipulation and gripper engineering — warehouse-picking, food-handling, and collaborative-robot
teams.
// how it works
BUILD NOTE
A servo-driven parallel or fin-ray (compliant) gripper printed from an open design is enough. Put the force sensor in a
fingertip pad, and remember the sensor reads a squeeze, not a mass — you are controlling grip force, not measuring
weight.
Sensing touch: A force-sensitive resistor (FSR) drops in resistance as you press it; a load cell flexes and changes a
strain-gauge bridge. Either gives you a voltage that rises with grip force at the fingertip.
Position vs force control: A position-controlled gripper closes to a set opening regardless of what is in it — fine for rigid
parts, disastrous for fragile ones. Force control closes until the fingertip force reaches a setpoint, then holds, adapting to
any object.
Compliance helps: Flexible fingers (fin-ray or soft pads) conform to an object’s shape, spreading contact and forgiving
errors. Mechanical compliance does half the work before the control loop even acts.
Grasp detection: A rising force signal tells you contact happened; a stable force tells you the grasp is secure; a sudden
drop tells you the object slipped. Reading these events is how a robot knows what its hand is doing.
The control loop: Command the servo to close, read fingertip force, and stop (or servo around) at the target force. Set a
low target for an egg, a higher one for a tool — the same gripper, different objects.

■ P R O J E C T 0 5
Force-Sensing Gripper
A gripper that feels how hard it's squeezing — grab an egg without breaking it

$40
intermediate
1 weekend
// why this matters
A gripper that only knows its finger position will crush a strawberry and drop a coffee cup. Give it a sense of touch — a force
sensor in the fingertip and a control loop on grip force — and it can pick up an egg, a paper cup, or a tool with just the right

squeeze. Building one teaches force sensing, compliant mechanisms, and force control as opposed to position control,
which is the difference between industrial pick-and-place and robots that can handle the messy, fragile real world. It is a
compact, satisfying build with an unforgettable demo.

build robots — a Build List field guide
12 / 15
WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand odometry and its drift, LiDAR scanning, SLAM at a conceptual and practical level (scan matching,
pose estimation, occupancy grids), and path planning on a real robot — the complete autonomy stack of mobile
robotics, and one of the most in-demand skill sets in the field.

→the job this maps to: autonomous-navigation and SLAM engineering — robot-vacuum, warehouse-AMR, delivery-robot,
and autonomy teams.
// how it works
BUILD NOTE
Use the tooling: a Raspberry Pi running ROS 2 with a cheap 2D LiDAR (RPLidar A1 or LD19) and the slam_toolbox
and Nav2 packages gets you a working map and navigation without writing SLAM from scratch. Learn what the
packages do first; go deeper on the algorithms once it drives.
Odometry, and why it drifts: Counting wheel rotations gives you a position estimate, but wheel slip and small errors
accumulate, so odometry alone wanders off within metres. It is a good short-term guess and a bad long-term truth.
LiDAR scans the room: A spinning 2D LiDAR returns hundreds of range measurements per revolution — a slice of the
surrounding walls. Each scan is a snapshot of what the world looks like from where the robot is.
SLAM: scan matching: SLAM compares each new scan to the map so far, finds the pose that best aligns them, corrects
the odometry drift, and adds the scan to the map. Localisation and mapping improve each other — the “simultaneous” in
SLAM.
The occupancy grid: The map is a grid where each cell is free, occupied, or unknown, built up from the scans. That grid
is what the planner reasons over.
Planning and navigation: Given the map and a goal, a planner (A* over a costmap that inflates obstacles) finds a path,
and a local controller drives it while dodging anything new. The robot is now autonomous in a space it built its own
model of.

■ P R O J E C T 0 6
SLAM Mapping Rover
A rover that maps a room it has never seen, then navigates it — autonomy, for real

$95
advanced
2–3 weekends
// why this matters
The rover in project 1 wanders blind; this one knows where it is. Put a spinning LiDAR on a wheeled base, add wheel
odometry, and run SLAM — simultaneous localisation and mapping — and the robot builds a map of the room as it drives

while tracking its own position inside it. Then give it a goal and it plans a path around the furniture and drives there. This is
the technology in every robot vacuum and warehouse robot, and building it end to end is the capstone of this guide:
perception, estimation, mapping, and planning in one machine.

Build the base with odometry
Assemble a 2WD base with encoder motors, publish wheel odometry, and drive it in a square. Watch how the

Mount and read the LiDAR
Mount the LiDAR level on top and stream scans. Visualise a scan and confirm the room’s walls appear as you turn the

Run SLAM
Launch slam_toolbox with odometry and LiDAR, drive the robot slowly around the room, and watch the map build in
real time. Note how the pose stays locked even as odometry drifts.

Save the finished map, restart, and have the robot localise itself within it from its scans alone. This is the moment it
“knows where it is.”

Launch Nav2, click a goal on the map, and watch the robot plan a path around obstacles and drive there. Drop
something in its way and watch it re-plan — autonomy achieved.

build robots — a Build List field guide
14 / 15

■ W R A P
Every robot is the same loop:
sense, decide, act.
A rover that avoids walls, an arm that reaches a coordinate, a quadruped that walks, a robot that sees and follows, a hand
that feels, a rover that maps its own world — six robots, one loop, escalating from reflexes to real autonomy. The parts are
commodity (servos, a LiDAR, a Pi); the skill is in the integration — the kinematics, the control loops, the perception, the
estimation. That is exactly what robotics teams hire for: people who can make the whole loop work on real hardware.
// the skill ladder
Build them in order and each one hands you the technique the next one needs:
reactive control →kinematics →locomotion →perception →force control →SLAM & navigation

!
BEFORE YOU POWER IT UP
Servos and motors pinch and draw serious current, and LiPo batteries need respect. Set current limits, keep fingers
clear of legs and grippers under power, never leave a LiPo charging unattended, power down before you rewire, and
test the quadruped and rovers in a clear area away from stairs and pets.
DO THIS
Build even one. Film it — a rover roaming, an arm placing an object, a quadruped’s first steps, a gripper lifting an egg,
a map drawing itself — and put the code on GitHub with your kinematics, your tuning, and an honest note on what
works and what doesn’t. One robot demo and one clean repo prove you can make the whole loop work.
Full build notes, parts links, and the next field guide go out in The Build List. The people actually shipping these —
and trading IK and gait tricks — are in Ohm’s Club.
